One deviation from the registered analysis plan was made for H3 and is transparently reported and justified in the Analytic Strategy.

Design & Participants

This study utilised a longitudinal, correlational design and there were no experimental conditions: participants completed a self-report measure of trait depressive symptoms on Day 1, followed by repeated measures of their momentary affective state and SMU style over three days. Our sample size was determined by available funding: we aimed to recruit 223 participants with expected attrition over the three days. A sensitivity analysis conducted in G*Power (Faul et al., 2007) indicated that this sample size provided 80% power to detect a one-tailed correlation of r ≥ .17 at α = .05 (see "Sample Size": https://osf.io/b9js3). Effect sizes of this magnitude were considered meaningful based on previous reviews reporting similar associations between active and passive SMU and indices of wellbeing (Godard & Holtzman, 2024; Valkenburg et al., 2021) that are unlikely to represent 'crud' factors (Ferguson & Heene, 2021; Orben & Lakens, 2020).

Participants were recruited via Prolific Academic (http://www.prolific.com/) -a crowdsourcing platform that yields high-quality data (Palan & Schitter, 2017; Peer et al., 2017).

Participants were eligible if they: (1) were aged 18-25 years; (2) resided in the United Kingdom; (3) were fluent in English; (4) reported no previous or current psychiatric diagnosis; (5) used social media frequently; (6) could complete the study on a desktop or laptop computer; and (7) were available to participate across three separate days.

The psychiatric-diagnosis criterion was implemented in accordance with the study's ethical approval. Prolific's prescreening tool was used to restrict study visibility accordingly, and eligibility was confirmed again during consent.

Questionnaire data were collected using Qualtrics (Qualtrics, Provo, UT), while the SNSBT was programmed in PsychoPy (Peirce et al., 2019) and hosted online via Pavlovia.

Participants could therefore be excluded at each assessment because of incomplete questionnaire and/or SNSBT data, as detailed in Figure 1. A total of 233 participants were recruited on Day 1 of the study and reinvited on Days 2 and 3. On Day 1, 13 participants were excluded resulting in usable data from 220 participants; on Day 2, 192 participants took part but 8 were excluded resulting in usable data from 184 participants; and on Day 3, 175 participants took part but 6 were excluded resulting in data from 169 participants. The final sample comprised 229 unique participants (Mage = 22.60, SD = 1.89) who provided usable data at one or more of the three timepoints. Using Prolific's quota sampling, we recruited an approximately equal number of female (n = 110) and male (n = 109) participants; one participant identified as non-binary and nine did not report their gender.

Most participants identified as White (61.8%), followed by Asian (17.2%), Other (6.8%), Black (6%), with some reporting that they did not identify with the ethnicities listed (6.8%) and 1.4% choosing not to report this. This study was approved by the Research Ethics Committee at Aston University (REF: HLS21157) and all participants provided informed consent. Participants were reimbursed with a £2.00 payment for ~20 minutes of their time on each testing day, equivalent to a rate of £6.00 per hour.

Measures

State Affect

The I-PANAS-SF (Thompson, 2007) measured state affect. This self-report questionnaire comprises 10 items which ask participants about their current positive and negative affect by indicating "the extent to which they feel each of the following in this moment" on a 6-point Likert scale anchored between 0 (Never) and 5 (Always). Five of the items measured positive affect (Alert, Inspired, Determined, Attentive, Active) and five measured negative affect (Upset, Hostile, Ashamed, Nervous, Afraid). Participants completed this questionnaire on each of the three days, so we replaced the Likert-style scale with a non-numerical sliding scale to mitigate recall bias. Both the positive affect subscale (McDonald's ω = .84) and the negative affect subscale (ω = .81) demonstrated excellent internal consistency across the three days.

Two composite scores were computed: the 5 positive items were summed to create a total score for positive affect and the 5 negative items to create a total score for negative affect. Scores for each sub-scale can range from 0 to 25 with higher scores corresponding to greater positive and negative affect, respectively.

Trait Depressive Symptoms

The MTSD (Chiappelli et al., 2014) comprises separate state and trait items; the present study administered 17 of the 18 trait items, which assess the frequency of depressive symptoms generally experienced in adulthood, excluding the previous week. The item assessing suicidal thoughts was omitted in accordance with the study's ethical approval. Participants respond to questions (e.g., "I felt sluggish and slow most of my life") on a 5-point Likert scale anchored between 0 (Never) and 4 (Experienced many times in a month for almost every month of my adult life). The MTSD demonstrated excellent internal consistency (ω = .93) and a total score for trait depression was computed by summing the 17 questions.

Social Media Use Style

An adapted version of the SNSBT (Shaw et al., 2022) was employed to measure distinct styles of SMU. The SNSBT has demonstrated evidence of convergent validity, with task-derived SMU styles corresponding with a self-report measure of active-passive SMU (Shaw et al., 2022). On each day, participants viewed a different set of 97 posts from an ostensible social network, comprising 90 images from the Nencki Affective Picture System (NAPS; Marchewka et al., 2013) and seven royalty-free TikTok-style videos (https://www.pexels.com/). The NAPS images depicted animals, objects, faces, people, and landscapes of positive or moderately negative valence. All participants viewed the same stimulus set on a given day, and the NAPS images were matched across the three sets on normative valence and arousal ratings to minimise systematic differences in image characteristics across assessment days. Participants were instructed to respond to each post as they typically would when using social media. They could 'Like' the post, which superimposed a heart icon over the content, 'Share' it with the ostensible social network, after which they received comments on the shared post, or select 'Next' to scroll to the subsequent post. For each assessment, the proportions of Like, Share and Next responses were calculated. These response proportions were subsequently combined using PCA to derive the SMU-style component score described in the Analytic Strategy.

Higher scores on this component reflect relatively greater interactive responding (Like and Share) and lower scores reflect relatively greater passive responding (Next responses).

Attention Checks

To control for careless responding that can substantially impact data quality (Stosic et al., 2024), two attention checks were included. On Day 1, an attention-check item was embedded among the MTSD items, stating: "This is an attention check. Please choose 'Never' as your response." On each day, a second attention check asked participants to respond to the multiplechoice question, "What planet do you live on?" by choosing one of four responses: Earth, Mars, Mercury, Saturn (Curran & Hauser, 2019; Jones et al., 2022). All participants passed these attention checks.

Procedure

On Day 1, participants completed two questionnaires administered in a randomised order: the I-PANAS-SF (Thompson, 2007) measured participants' state positive and negative affect, and the 17 trait-based items of the MTSD (Chiappelli et al., 2014) measured trait depression. After completing these questionnaires, participants completed the SNSBT. On Days 2 and 3, participants completed the I-PANAS-SF and then the SNSBT. Each daily assessment took approximately 20 minutes. 2 provides a schematic example of the procedure. Note. * = Only presented on Day 1.

Analytic Strategy

All analyses were conducted in Jamovi (v2.5; The Jamovi Project, 2024) with an alpha level of .05. To derive a composite index of SMU style from responses on the SNSBT, we first performed a Principal Component Analysis (PCA) on the proportions of Like, Share, and Next responses. This yielded a one-component solution accounting for 76.4% of the variance. Like and Share responses loaded positively and Next responses negatively, such that higher component scores indicated more interactive SMU and lower scores indicated more passive SMU style. This component score was used as the dependent variable in the subsequent confirmatory analyses.

Linear mixed-effects models were conducted for H1-H3 using the GAMLj package (v3; Gallucci, 2023) with Restricted Maximum Likelihood Estimation (REML). Mixed-effects models accommodate unequal numbers of observations and missing repeated measurements (Detry & Ma, 2016; Hayes, 2006; Quené & Van Den Bergh, 2004). Prior to hypothesis testing, an unconditional model with participant (ID) included as a random intercept was fitted to estimate the intraclass correlation coefficient (ICC) and quantify the proportion of variance in SMU style attributable to between-person differences. Participant was subsequently retained as a random intercept in all hypothesis-testing models to account for the non-independence of repeated observations nested within individuals.

For H1 and H2, which examined associations between positive and negative affect and SMU style, we compared random-intercept models with models additionally including participant-specific random slopes for affect, as specified in the registered analysis plan. Model fit was compared using likelihood ratio tests (LRTs), Akaike Information Criterion (AIC; Akaike, 1974), and Bayesian Information Criterion (BIC; Schwarz, 1978) to determine whether allowing the association between affect and SMU style to vary across participants improved model fit.

For H3, the registered analysis plan specified a linear regression examining the relationship between trait depression and SMU style. We deviated from this plan because a linear mixed-effects model more appropriately reflected the repeated-measures structure of the data, with SMU-style observations nested within participants across the three study days. H3 was therefore tested using a linear mixed-effects model with trait depression as a time-invariant participant-level predictor. Trait depression was assessed on Day 1 and the resulting score was applied to each available repeated observation for that participant, allowing all available SMU observations to contribute while accounting for their non-independence.

Results

A total of N = 220 participants provided usable data on Day 1, with n = 184 on Day 2, and n = 16 9 on Day 3. There were 149 participants with data across all three timepoints, n = 46 with two timepoints, and n = 34 with one timepoint, resulting in 573 observations overall from 229 unique participants. The number of observations contributing to individual analyses varied according to missing data. Table 1 shows descriptive statistics for all study variables.

Participants generally exhibited more passive ("Next") rather than interactive ("Like", "Share") behaviour on the SNSBT, consistent with findings from previous research using the SNSBT (Shaw et al., 2022) and self-report active-passive measures (Escobar-Viera et al., 2018; Pempek et al., 2009). On average, participants also reported more positive than negative affect on the I-PANAS-SF.

Momentary Affect & Social Media Usage Style

An intercept-only linear mixed model with PCA of the SNSBT scores as the outcome and participant as a random intercept indicated an intraclass correlation coefficient (ICC) of .88.

This indicated that approximately 88% of the variance in SMU style was attributable to differences between participants, justifying the use of a multilevel model. For positive affect, adding a participant-specific random slope significantly improved model fit over the randomintercept model, LRT(2) = 25.32, p < .001, with lower AIC and BIC values. The randomintercept and random-slope model was therefore retained. For negative affect, adding a random slope did not improve model fit, LRT(2) = 0.23, p = .89, and the random-intercept model was retained. Table 2 provides these estimates. Accordingly, the positive-affect association is reported from the random-intercept and random-slope model (Model 2), whereas the negativeaffect association is reported from the random-intercept model (Model 1).

In support of H1, there was a significant positive relationship between positive affect and SMU style, b = .05, SE = .01, 95% CI [.03, .08], t(143) = 3.72, p < .001. The full mixedeffects model explained 90% of the variance in SMU style (conditional R² = .90), with the fixed effect of positive affect accounting for approximately 2% of the variance (marginal R² = .02).

Contrary to H2, there was no significant relationship between negative affect and SMU style, b = -.02, SE = .02, 95% CI [-.06, .02], t(490) = -1.13, p = .26. The fixed effect of negative affect accounted for less than 1% of the variance in SMU style (marginal R² = .001). Across the three assessment days, higher positive affect was therefore associated with a more interactive SMU style, whereas negative affect was not significantly associated with SMU style (Figure 3). Note. Left Panel = Positive Affect, Right Panel = Negative Affect. Connecting lines link observations from the same participant across measurement occasions. The red line denotes the model-estimated association.

Trait Depressive Symptoms & Social Media Usage Style

Contrary to H3, trait depressive symptoms were not associated with SMU style across repeated assessments, b = .01, SE = .01, 95% CI [-.01, .04], t(219) = 1.21, p = .23. The fixed effect of trait depressive symptoms explained less than 1% of the variance in SMU style (marginal R² = .006). This analysis included 559 observations from 220 participants.

Exploratory Analyses

Given the null association between trait depressive symptoms and SMU style, non-registered exploratory analyses were conducted to examine whether trait depressive symptoms showed the expected associations with positive and negative affect. Exploratory linear regression analyses indicated that trait depressive symptoms were negatively related to self-reported positive affect, b = -.09, SE = .03, 95% CI [-.14, -.04], t(218) = -3.52, p < .001, R² = .05, and positively related to negative affect, b = .10, SE = .02, 95% CI [.06, .13], t(218) = 5.10, p < .001, R² = .11.

Discussion

Growing concerns about young people's mental health have coincided with the widespread use of social media, prompting researchers and policymakers to examine how SMU relates to wellbeing. Prior research, however, has been limited by a reliance on cross-sectional self-report data, a focus on usage quantity rather than how people engage with social media, and limited consideration of individual differences. Addressing these limitations, the present study combined a direct behavioural measure of SMU style with an EMA design to examine associations with state positive and negative affect and trait depressive symptoms. Across three days, higher positive affect was associated with more interactive SMU style, whereas negative affect and trait depressive symptoms were not significantly associated with SMU style. SMU style showed substantial between-person differences and considerable consistency within individuals across repeated assessments. Together, these findings suggest that relatively stable individual differences in SMU style coexist with a modest association between positive affect and more interactive behaviour.

In support of our first hypothesis, higher positive affect was associated with more interactive SMU on the SNSBT. This finding is consistent with previous research indicating that active SMU is associated with more positive affective experiences, although these associations are generally small (Godard & Holtzman, 2024; Tuck & Thompson, 2024; Verduyn et al., 2017). Mood Management Theory provides one possible account of this association, proposing that media engagement is partly shaped by current affective states and motivations to maintain or regulate affect (Reinecke, 2017; Zillmann, 1988). Within the SNSBT, higher positive affect may therefore have been associated with greater readiness to engage with available content through liking and sharing rather than scrolling. This pattern is also consistent with the Differential Susceptibility to Media Effects Model (Valkenburg & Peter, 2013; Valkenburg et al., 2015), whereby relatively consistent person-level tendencies in media engagement may coexist with more proximal associations involving affective state.

Contrary to H2, negative affect was not significantly associated with SMU style.

Although we hypothesised that higher negative affect would be associated with less interactive SMU, Mood Management Theory allows for more heterogeneous behavioural responses to negative affect. One possibility is that negative affect may be associated with withdrawal or passive consumption for some individuals, whereas for others it may motivate active engagement aimed at regulating mood or seeking social support or connection (Reinecke, 2017; Zillmann, 1988; see also Fassi et al., 2025; Jarman et al., 2021; Nesi et al., 2018 Nesi et al., , 2020)). Such divergent responses could obscure a consistent association between negative affect and SMU style at the group level, consistent with evidence that associations between active and passive SMU and affect vary across individuals and contexts (Beyens et al., 2021; Godard & Holtzman, 2024; Tuck & Thompson, 2024). However, the absence of a significant random slope for negative affect in the present study provides little evidence that this association varied systematically between participants within the SNSBT.

The characteristics of the SNSBT may therefore also help explain the absence of an association with negative affect. Although liking, sharing, and scrolling emulate common social-media behaviours, the task does not capture the full range of behaviours through which negative affect might shape naturalistic SMU. Negative affect may, for example, be more closely associated with monitoring social feedback, engaging in social comparison, seeking reassurance, selectively engaging with select content, or posting about personal experiences (Fassi et al., 2025; Jarman et al., 2021; Nesi et al., 2018 Nesi et al., , 2020)). Negative affect instead be more associated with particular motivations, content, or social contexts than with a general tendency towards interactive versus passive responding. This interpretation is consistent with broader theoretical accounts emphasising the importance of specific mechanisms, contexts, and individual differences in understanding social-media effects (Maheux et al., 2024; Orben et al., 2024).

Contrary to our final hypothesis, trait depressive symptoms were not associated with SMU style, explaining less than 1% of variance. This finding differs from previous crosssectional research showing that greater passive SMU is associated with higher depressive symptoms, whereas greater active SMU is associated with lower depressive symptoms (Escobar-Viera et al., 2018). However, this comparison should be treated cautiously because Escobar-Viera et al. relied on self-reported SMU, whereas the present study measured behavioural responding directly within the SNSBT. Furthermore, participants reporting a current or previous psychiatric diagnosis were excluded from the present study, which may have restricted variability in trait depressive symptoms and our ability to detect an association with SMU style. Accordingly, the null finding should not be interpreted as evidence that depressive symptoms are unrelated to patterns of social media engagement, particularly among individuals experiencing clinically significant depression (see Politte-Corn et al., 2024; Primack et al., 2021). More broadly, our findings suggest that momentary positive affect and trait depressive symptoms show different patterns of association with behavioural responding on the SNSBT. Whereas trait depressive symptoms were unrelated to SMU style in this nonclinical sample, higher positive affect was associated with greater interactive responding. This reinforces the importance of considering both proximal affective states and more enduring psychological characteristics when examining social media behaviour, while recognising that their associations may depend on the population and context under study.

Limitations & Future Research Directions

Several limitations should be considered when interpreting these findings. Although the study employed a longitudinal EMA design, it cannot establish causality between affect and SMU style. Affect was measured before participants completed the SNSBT on each testing day, which provides some temporal ordering. However, the data remain correlational in nature.

Future research should therefore employ experimental designs capable of testing causal mechanisms more directly. One promising approach would be to manipulate participants' affective states through the valence of social media content or established affect-induction procedures before assessing SMU. For example, if exposure to positively valenced content increases positive affect, participants may subsequently engage in more interactive behaviours, whereas exposure to negatively valenced content may increase negative affect or reduce positive affect, leading to different patterns of engagement (Brady et al., 2025; De Valle et al., 2021; Stiff & Orchard, 2025). Such approaches would help establish whether affective states causally influence social media behaviour, whether social media experiences shape affect, or whether these processes operate bidirectionally over time.

Second, although the SNSBT was developed to capture behavioural features common to social media platforms, it necessarily provides a simplified and standardised representation of real-world SMU. Participants respond to standardised content from an ostensible social network rather than content originating from their own social networks, and comments received after sharing are simulated rather than provided by their own social contacts. Consequently, the task constrains many of the relational and contextual factors that may shape naturalistic SMU, including relationship history, audience composition, perceived visibility and social consequences of engagement, and the personal relevance of content and feedback. From an affordances perspective, SMU behaviour emerges partly from the possibilities for action provided by particular platforms and how these are experienced by individual users (Bayer et al., 2020; Valkenburg, 2022). Platform norms and affordances, use motivations, and interpersonal context may therefore influence decisions to like, share, or scroll past content in ways that are deliberately constrained within the SNSBT to increase experimental control, but necessarily limit its ecological validity.

POSITIVE AFFECT AND INTERACTIVE SOCIAL MEDIA USE

These limitations highlight a broader challenge within social media research: balancing experimental control with ecological validity. The standardisation afforded by the SNSBT enables behavioural choices to be compared across participants within a common stimulus environment, but necessarily constrains the personalised, interpersonal, and platform-specific factors that shape naturalistic SMU. Future research that triangulates controlled behavioural tasks, digital trace data, and intensive longitudinal methods may provide a more comprehensive understanding of how affective states, platform features, and individual differences interact to shape social media behaviour and wellbeing.

Conclusion

The present study examined associations between SMU style and state and trait indicators of wellbeing. SMU style showed considerable consistency across repeated assessments, alongside a modest association between higher positive affect and more interactive SMU. Negative affect and trait depressive symptoms were not significantly associated with SMU style. Together, these findings suggest that relatively stable individual differences in SMU style coexist with a modest association between positive affect and interactive behaviour. By extending a literature that has often relied on retrospective self-report measures of SMU frequency and style, this study highlights the value of direct behavioural measurement and longitudinal approaches for capturing both individual differences and variation over time in social media behaviour.
